intro.title: Explore Lagunas de Zempoala National Park
intro.description: Lagunas de Zempoala National Park is located on the border between State of Mexico and Morelos, not far from Mexico City. It is the main recharge area of the Apatlaco River micro-basin aquifer. The lagoons and coniferous forests create breathtaking scenery. It is also the only place in Morelos where the ocelot (Leopardus pardalis) has been recorded. The park covers 4,790 hectares and was established by decree on November 27, 1936.

visitGuide.title: Visiting Tips
items: Park open Saturday, Sunday and public holidays, morning arrival recommended
Entrance fee 95 MXN per person, free for children under 12
Wear comfortable walking shoes, most areas are walkable, horse rental available
Cold climate in fall/winter, mild in spring/summer, bring appropriate clothing

alsoKnownAs.title: Highlights
items: Seven Lagoons: Zempoala means 'many lagoons' in Nahuatl. The park features seven lagoons — Quila, Zempoala, Compila, Tonatiwha, Seca, Prieta and Huilapan. Only three are permanent; the rest are intermittent depending on rainfall.
Rare Species: The only place in Morelos where the ocelot (Leopardus pardalis) has been recorded, along with endemic species like the cross-banded rattlesnake (Crotalus transversus).
Aquifer Recharge: The main recharge area of the Apatlaco River micro-basin aquifer, one of the few perennial water bodies near the Mexico City metropolitan area.
Ecotourism: Activities include camping, hiking, landscape meditation, nature photography, wildlife observation and sport fishing.

route.title: Tour Route
route.overview: Discover the ideal route to explore Lagunas de Zempoala National Park and experience the breathtaking scenery of lagoons and coniferous forests.
steps: Depart from Mexico City in the morning via Federal Highway 95 toward Cuernavaca, about 2 hours to the park entrance.
Upon arrival, visit the visitor center to learn about the park's ecosystem, seven lagoons and conservation information.
Hike along the interpretive trails, enjoy the lagoons and surrounding coniferous forests, and observe wildlife.
Rest at the viewpoints by the lake and take in the breathtaking scenery of lagoons and forests. Most areas are walkable, horse rental is also available.
supplements: Park is at high altitude — cold in fall/winter, mild in spring/summer, bring warm clothes.
Park only open on weekends and public holidays, please plan your trip in advance.
Park facilities include restrooms, viewpoints, information modules and interpretive trails.
Budget-friendly restaurants and camping areas near the park, recommend bringing your own food and water.

sections.title: Historical Significance
sections.content: Lagunas de Zempoala National Park was established by federal decree on November 27, 1936, one of the earliest national parks in Mexico. The park spans Huitzilac in Morelos and Ocuilan in State of Mexico, covering 4,790 hectares. It protects the region's important freshwater lake ecosystem and coniferous forests, a model for natural conservation in Mexico.

sections.title: Natural Landscape
sections.content: The park features seven lagoons surrounded by Montezuma pine forests. Three are perennial lagoons (Quila, Zempoala, Compila), while the remaining four are intermittent, depending on rainfall. It is the only place in Morelos where the ocelot (Leopardus pardalis) has been recorded, along with endemic species such as the cross-banded rattlesnake (Crotalus transversus) and the Mexican salamander (Ambystoma altamirani). Other representative species include bobcat (Lynx rufus), raccoon (Procyon lotor), and Steller's jay (Cyanocitta stelleri).

sections.title: Visiting Experience
sections.content: Visiting Lagunas de Zempoala National Park is an unforgettable natural experience. You can hike the interpretive trails around the lagoons, go bird watching, camp, or practice landscape meditation by the lake. The park also offers environmental education activities and nature photography opportunities. Most areas are walkable, but horse rental is available. Park facilities include a visitor center, viewpoints, information modules, restrooms, interpretive trails and a craft shop.

sections.title: Park Rules (ANP)
sections.content:
1. Be a responsible and environmentally friendly visitor.
2. Upon entering Lagunas de Zempoala National Park, follow the instructions of the park rangers.
Let's protect this precious natural heritage together.

sections.title: Representative Flora and Fauna
sections.content: The park is home to a wide variety of flora and fauna. Animals include: bobcat (Lynx rufus), raccoon (Procyon lotor), Steller's jay (Cyanocitta stelleri), Trans-Volcanic rattlesnake (Crotalus triseriatus), Altamira's axolotl (Ambystoma altamirani), long-tailed wood-partridge (Dendrortyx macroura), cross-banded mountain rattlesnake (Crotalus transversus), and ocelot (Leopardus pardalis). Plants include: Montezuma pine (Pinus montezumae), large-leaf aster (Muhlenbergia macroura), southern cattail (Typha domingensis), and cardinal flower (Lobelia cardinalis).

officialManagement.title: About Lagunas de Zempoala National Park
officialManagement.text: Lagunas de Zempoala National Park is located on the border between State of Mexico and Morelos, established by decree on November 27, 1936, covering 4,790 hectares. It is the main recharge area of the Apatlaco River micro-basin aquifer and one of the few perennial water bodies near the Mexico City metropolitan area. Zempoala means 'many lagoons' in Nahuatl, and the park features seven lagoons. It is also the only place in Morelos where the ocelot (Leopardus pardalis) has been recorded.

historyTimeline.title: History and Nature Timeline

items.title: Name Origin: The Meaning of Zempoala
items.description: Zempoala means 'many lagoons' in Nahuatl, as the park features seven lagoons: Quila, Zempoala, Compila, Tonatiwha, Seca, Prieta, and Huilapan. Only three are perennial lagoons; the rest are intermittent, their appearance and formation of large water bodies depending on rainfall.

items.title: November 27, 1936: National Park Decree
items.description: Lagunas de Zempoala National Park was officially established by federal decree on November 27, 1936, becoming one of the earliest national parks in Mexico. The park spans Ocuilan in State of Mexico and Huitzilac in Morelos, covering 4,790 hectares, aimed at protecting this important freshwater lake ecosystem and coniferous forests.

items.title: Unique Ecosystem: Aquifer Recharge Area
items.description: The park is the main recharge area of the Apatlaco River micro-basin aquifer, one of the few perennial water bodies near the Mexico City metropolitan area. Dense forests, easy access, and three other natural protected areas in the region make it an important habitat for numerous endemic species, such as the cross-banded rattlesnake (Crotalus transversus).

items.title: Rare Species: Home of the Ocelot
items.description: This is the only place in Morelos where the ocelot (Leopardus pardalis) has been recorded. Other representative species include bobcat (Lynx rufus), raccoon (Procyon lotor), Steller's jay (Cyanocitta stelleri), Transverse Volcano rattlesnake (Crotalus triseriatus), Mexican salamander (Ambystoma altamirani), and Long-tailed Wood-partridge (Dendrortyx macroura).

items.title: Today: Ecotourism and Nature Conservation
items.description: Today, Lagunas de Zempoala National Park is an important ecotourism destination in Mexico. Visitors can enjoy camping, hiking, landscape meditation, environmental education, nature photography, wildlife observation and sport fishing. Park facilities include a visitor center, viewpoints, information modules, restrooms, interpretive trails and a craft shop. Please be a responsible and eco-friendly visitor, and follow the park rangers' instructions.

historyTimeline.guideContent: When visiting, start at the **Visitor Center** to learn about the park's ecosystem and seven lagoons; then hike the **Interpretive Trails** to enjoy the breathtaking scenery of lagoons and coniferous forests; rest at the **Viewpoints** to observe wildlife; and finally visit the **Craft Shop** for souvenirs. Please be a responsible and eco-friendly visitor, and follow the park rangers' instructions.

seoOverview.welcome: Welcome to **Lagunas de Zempoala National Park**, widely recognized as **Zempoala National Park**. Located in **Ocuilan**, **State of Mexico**, **Mexico** - on the border with **Morelos** - this national park is a primary hub for travelers exploring the lagoons, pine forests and rare wildlife of the region.

cards.heading: About Lagunas de Zempoala National Park
cards.text: Established in 1936, the park protects seven highland lagoons - Zempoala, Quila, Compila, Tonatiwha, Seca, Prieta and Huilapan - surrounded by Montezuma pine forests, and is one of the few places in Mexico where the rare axolotl and the ocelot can be found.

cards.heading: Location & How to Visit Zempoala National Park in Ocuilan
cards.text: Lagunas de Zempoala National Park is easy to visit from Mexico City via Federal Highway 95, about 20.3 km from Cuernavaca. The park opens Saturday, Sunday and public holidays from 09:00 to 18:00; plan your trip with the interactive map below.

cards.heading: Landmarks & Attractions Around Zempoala National Park
cards.text: When visiting **Lagunas de Zempoala National Park**, travelers can easily explore surrounding landmarks and points of interest, including **Cuernavaca**, with its historic center and cathedral, and the **pueblo mágico** of **Tepoztlán**, home to the Tepozteco pyramid. The **Pico del Águila** viewpoint lies along the same highway.

cards.heading: History & Significance of Lagunas de Zempoala National Park
cards.text: Created by federal decree on 27 November 1936, the park covers 4,790 hectares between Ocuilan (State of Mexico) and Huitzilac (Morelos). It is the main recharge area of the Apatlaco River micro-basin aquifer and one of the few perennial water bodies near the Mexico City metropolitan area.

faqSection.title: Frequently Asked Questions about Lagunas de Zempoala National Park
faqSection.subtitle: Everything you need to know before visiting Zempoala National Park in Ocuilan, State of Mexico.

items.q: Where is Lagunas de Zempoala National Park located?
items.a: Lagunas de Zempoala National Park is located in Ocuilan, State of Mexico, Mexico, on the border with Morelos - about 20.3 km from Cuernavaca and a two-hour drive from Mexico City.

items.q: Is Zempoala National Park free to visit?
items.a: No. Lagunas de Zempoala National Park charges an entrance fee of 95 MXN per person per day. Children under 12, seniors, retirees and visitors with disabilities enter free with valid ID, while students and teachers receive a 75% discount.

items.q: When is Lagunas de Zempoala National Park open?
items.a: Zempoala National Park is open on Saturday, Sunday and public holidays from 09:00 to 18:00, and is closed from Monday to Friday.

items.q: What can you do at Lagunas de Zempoala National Park?
items.a: Visitors can enjoy camping, hiking, birdwatching, nature photography, sport fishing, landscape meditation and environmental education among the seven lagoons of the park in Ocuilan, State of Mexico.

items.q: Which wildlife can you see at Lagunas de Zempoala National Park?
items.a: The park is home to rare species such as the ocelot (Leopardus pardalis), the cross-banded rattlesnake (Crotalus transversus) and the Mexican axolotl (Ambystoma altamirani), together with Montezuma pine forests.

items.q: How do you get to Lagunas de Zempoala National Park from Mexico City?
items.a: Drive along Federal Highway 95 (Mexico-Cuernavaca) and follow the signed access road to the park, roughly two hours from Mexico City and 20.3 km from Cuernavaca.

items.q: What attractions are near Lagunas de Zempoala National Park?
items.a: Nearby landmarks include Cuernavaca with its cathedral and historic center, Tepoztlán with the Tepozteco pyramid, and the Pico del Águila viewpoint.

weather.title: Weather & 7-Day Forecast
weather.subtitle: Live conditions for the lagoon zone at about 2,800 m above sea level. Mountain weather can change within an hour - check before you set off.
weather.tip: Open days are weekends and public holidays (09:00-18:00). Cold mornings and sudden rain are common; bring layers and a light rain jacket.
weather.unavailable: Live forecast is temporarily unavailable. Please refresh the page later.
weather.fallbackNone: No special conditions today. At 2,800 m the weather can change within an hour - check the forecast before heading up.
weather.aSunny: Clear sky: start early for calm lagoon water and the best photo light.
weather.aCloudy: Overcast: soft light for photos and comfortable long walks without direct sun.
weather.aFog: Fog is possible: viewpoints may be clouded in; it usually lifts around midday.
weather.aRainPlan: High rain chance later: do the trails in the morning and keep a plan B under the picnic ramadas.
weather.aRainNow: It's raining now: trails are slippery; stick to the main paths and the lagoon shore.
weather.aHotDay: Warm day: avoid 12:00-16:00 sun, hike in forest shade and take breaks.
weather.aWindNote: Noticeable wind by the lagoons and ridges: viewpoints feel colder - keep your hat secure.
weather.cLayers: Big temperature swing: dress in layers and shed one at midday.
weather.cCold: Cold day (mornings below 10 °C): warm jacket, beanie and light gloves.
weather.cHot: Warm at 2,800 m: light breathable clothes plus a loose long sleeve for sun cover.
weather.cRainGear: Light waterproof jacket and grip footwear - trails wet up fast.
weather.cWindBreak: Light windbreaker: open areas feel several degrees colder in the wind.
weather.iPoncho: Compact poncho or rain jacket plus a cover for your backpack.
weather.iSunscreen: Strong high-altitude sun: SPF50+ sunscreen, sunglasses and a hat.
weather.iWater: Water (1 L per person) - dehydration creeps up on you at altitude.
weather.iExtraLayer: One extra warm layer in the pack for cold mornings.
weather.iPoles: If it's muddy, light trekking poles help on the way down to the lagoons.
weather.riskStorm: Thunderstorm: leave open ridges, lagoon shores and lone trees - consider postponing the hike.
weather.riskHeavyRain: Heavy rain: avoid ravines and low ground - trails can briefly turn into streams.
weather.riskWind: Strong gusty wind: use caution on exposed ridges and open trails.
weather.riskIce: Possible ice on shaded trails: wear grippy footwear and walk slowly.

seasonalGuide.title: Seasonal Visiting Strategy
seasonalGuide.subtitle: A practical table based on the region's long-term climate, hydrology and wildlife patterns. Weather varies from day to day - always confirm with the live forecast before travelling.

rows.weather: Clear, dry days with very cold mornings and nights; night frost possible.
rows.water: Permanent lagoons remain at a stable, lower level; seasonal lagoons are mostly dry or very shallow.
rows.wildlife: Birds gather at the water at sunrise; footprints of mammals can be found along the shores.
rows.tips: Best for crisp photo light. Bring layers, gloves and sun protection; arrive by late morning for the warmest hours.

rows.weather: Warmest and driest months; strong sun and a higher fire risk in the pine forest.
rows.water: Water levels keep receding; some seasonal basins can dry out completely by late May.
rows.wildlife: Best in the early morning and late afternoon; reptiles bask in the sun and bird song increases.
rows.tips: Start very early and carry extra drinking water. Strictly respect fire rules and stay on marked trails.

rows.weather: Mild days with frequent afternoon showers or thunderstorms and sudden temperature drops.
rows.water: The lagoons refill and look their fullest; seasonal lagoons reappear.
rows.wildlife: Amphibians such as salamanders become active and breed - look, but never touch or disturb them.
rows.tips: Waterproof shoes, a rain jacket and quick-dry clothes. Trails can be slippery; allow extra time.

rows.weather: Rain gradually eases; crisp, clear mornings with occasional drizzle.
rows.water: Full water levels early in the season, then slowly stabilising.
rows.wildlife: Migration season - excellent for birdwatching; wildlife remains active before winter.
rows.tips: Fewer visitors and beautiful light for photography. Mornings are cool - carry a light jacket.

storySection.title: The Story Behind the Lagoons
storySection.subtitle: Name, memory and conservation - the threads that connect these lagoons to the people who lived beside them.

cards.title: What Zempoala Means
cards.text: Zempoala comes from the Nahuatl word for "place of many waters" or "twenty waters". The name echoes in several towns of central Mexico and here it points to a landscape once dotted with far more water bodies than the seven that survive today.

cards.title: The Legend of Zempoatl
cards.text: According to an oral tradition retold by the National Water Commission (CONAGUA), Zempoatl was a young woman of Huitzilac whose story of love and loss ended in tears. Her grieving father and brothers wept day and night, and their tears filled the valley - giving life to the lagoons that still mirror the sky today. The park's name and the legend meet in the same idea: this is a place born of water.

cards.title: A Protected Landscape Since 1936
cards.text: The lagoons were declared Lagunas de Zempoala National Park in 1936 - one of the first national parks in Mexico - protecting almost 4,790 hectares of lagoons and Montezuma pine forest across the State of Mexico and Morelos. The decree was later adjusted in 1947 to define today's protected area.

conservation.title: Science Corner & Visitor Responsibilities
conservation.subtitle: A national park is a living laboratory. Understanding why these lagoons exist helps us visit without leaving a mark.

topics.title: Lakes born in a volcanic land
topics.text: The lagoons occupy natural depressions of an ancient volcanic landscape in the Sierra de Ajusco-Chichinauhtzin at about 2,800 m. Rain and thin volcanic soils slowly feed the basins, which is why the area is one of the few permanent water bodies close to Mexico City.

topics.title: Why some lagoons appear and disappear
topics.text: Only three lagoons are permanent (Quila, Zempoala, Compila); the other four are seasonal. They fill when the summer rains arrive and shrink or vanish in the dry season - a natural rhythm, not a sign of damage.

topics.title: Why the axolotl is so rare
topics.text: The Mexican salamander (Ambystoma altamirani) lives only in this mountain region. Habitat loss, water pollution, introduced predatory fish, and collection for the pet trade have pushed it to the edge. Seeing one here is a privilege - and a reason to stay quiet and keep the water clean.

topics.title: The forest that stores the water
topics.text: Montezuma pines and mixed forest act as a giant sponge: they capture fog and rain, slow the runoff and recharge the aquifer below. Protecting trees is protecting the lagoons themselves.

rules: Walk only on marked trails and never disturb signs, fences or equipment.
Camp only in designated areas; fires are allowed only where authorised.
Never feed, chase or touch wildlife - including horses and birds.
Do not take plants, animals, stones or water from the park.
Carry all rubbish out with you, especially plastic and glass.
Keep noise low so wildlife and other visitors can enjoy the silence.
Leave the lagoons untouched: no washing, no waste, no chemicals.
Smoking is a fire risk in pine forest - follow the park's fire rules.
